newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Play parodies property-obsessed Singaporeans.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Play parodies property-obsessed Singaporeans.

text.p: Singapore's real estate boom has inspired a play parodying the city state's feverish rush to cash in on the trend.

Local playwright Eleanor Wong's latest work "Block Sale", which has had its first run this month, depicts the current appetite for bunching several properties into a single "block" offering for sale in the chase for millions of dollars in profits.

Through these sales, or "lottery strikes", sellers can earn two or three times more than they would get if they sold their units individually. In Singapore's expensive private property market, that can amount to a profit of millions of Singapore dollars.
The property craze has residents and property speculators joining forces to offload their units in old apartment buildings in block sales. The sites are redeveloped into larger condominiums.

"The whole phenomenon of a block sale presented the issue in a particularly acute fashion, because suddenly, being able to sell in a block sale presents very starkly the question of what is your house: is it just an asset to be sold to make money? Is the price the only consideration that should prevail when you are thinking about this?" Wong told Reuters in an interview.

"It also pits human beings against one another as you have this push and pull between different people who are suddenly joined at the hip, not by their own choice. The situation presented interesting opportunities for dramatic tension."

In the comedy, the residents of "Happy Valley Condominium" are drawn by a S$60 million (US$42.9 million) block sale proposition, into a web of greed and deception when one of them, an old lady, refuses to sell her family home.

Wong, a lawyer with an international law firm in addition to being a playwright, said: "You will only find the concept of condominiums.... in very land-scarce kinds of places. In big cities with suburbs, people either live in apartments in the city or in houses in the suburbs. You don't really have anything in between."
"By definition, for a block sale to be worthwhile for the developer, it has got to be a little cluster of low-rise apartments with a lot more space in between."
The phenomenon might not last for long, Wong said.
"Candidates for block sales will diminish as you are really talking about older developments that were built in (the days) when one believed in having space for a garden."
The nation's skyrocketing property prices of recent years and the accompanying money-making potential, accounts for Singapore's obsession with the sector.
"You cannot escape the reality of what the precipitous rise in property prices over the past few years means for Singaporeans," Wong said.

"In a way that is something people in other cities have come to grips with, but...for this generation (of Singaporeans) it is something that has happened within our lifetime and has changed the landscape of a person's ambition quite a lot," she said.
Property prices on the land-scarce island have eased off only in the past few months. In May, the government introduced a slate of measures aimed at cooling property speculation.

"In a country that prides itself on not having any class distinction, with the rise in prices, property ownership very clearly becomes the potential for creating class differences ... the objective facts drive you to becoming obsessed by it because if you are not, somebody is going to tell you are a fool," Wong said.
